hook: A cheque someone gave me bounced.

slides.title: It can be a criminal offence.
slides.body: If a cheque given to pay a legally enforceable debt bounces because the account doesn't have enough money (or it exceeds the limit arranged with the bank), the issuer can be punished.

slides.title: Step 1: Present it in time.
slides.body: The cheque must be presented within its validity period. Cheques are valid for 3 months from the date on them.
slides.ref: NI Act Sec 138, proviso (a) · RBI, Nov 2011

slides.title: Step 2: Send a written notice within 30 days.
slides.body: Once your bank tells you the cheque bounced, send the issuer a written demand for the money within 30 days.

slides.title: Step 3: Give them 15 days to pay.
slides.body: If the issuer doesn't pay within 15 days of receiving your notice, you can file a complaint.

slides.title: Step 4: File within one month.
slides.body: File the complaint in court within one month after those 15 days end. The court can allow a delay if you show sufficient cause.

slides.title: What the issuer can face.
slides.body: Jail of up to 2 years, a fine of up to twice the cheque amount, or both. During the case, the court may also order the issuer to pay interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount.

slides.title: Where to file.
slides.body: If you deposited the cheque through your bank account, file in the court for the area where your bank branch is.

sources: RBI notification, 4 Nov 2011: cheques valid for 3 months
caption:
Someone's cheque bounced on you? Here's what the law says. 👇

1️⃣ A cheque bouncing for lack of funds can be a criminal offence
2️⃣ Present it within its validity: 3 months from its date
3️⃣ Send a written notice within 30 days of the bank telling you
4️⃣ No payment within 15 days? File a complaint within the next month
5️⃣ Penalty: up to 2 years' jail and/or a fine up to twice the cheque amount

Source: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Sec 138, 142, 143A); RBI notification (Nov 2011)
